items.heading: Vestiges and the 1840s freeze on evolution

claims.text: Robert Chambers's anonymous Vestiges (1844) proposed a developmental law for species and was savaged by men of science Darwin respected. The main charge was that the author lacked the qualifications to speak on the origin of species.

citations.title: Chambers, Robert (1802-1871)
citations.author: Linda Hall Library
citations.quote: The public was excited and titillated by the Vestiges, but the scientific community was appalled, and a number of critical and often vitriolic reviews were published in literary journals

claims.text: The exhibit's reading is that this reception led Darwin to resolve that his own book could not be dismissed as unqualified, and to stay silent until his qualifications were impeccable. This explains the Origin's accumulation of facts and its caution.

citations.title: Chambers, Robert (1802-1871)
citations.author: Linda Hall Library
citations.quote: Darwin, surprised by the icy reception met with by the Vestiges, seems to have promised himself that when his book appeared, no one could accuse him of a lack of qualifications.

disagreement.summary: When did Wallace's essay reach Darwin, and did Darwin delay forwarding it? The Darwin Correspondence Project editors accept 18 June 1858; Brooks and McKinney argue for an earlier arrival.

sides.position: Darwin received the essay on 18 June 1858, as his letter to Lyell says (the editors' dating, following Francis Darwin and Lyell's endorsement).

claims.text: The editors date Darwin's letter to Lyell 18 June 1858, relying on Francis Darwin and on Lyell's endorsement of the letter.

sides.position: The letter arrived earlier (McKinney: 3 June; Brooks: possibly mid-May), so Darwin may have held it back and used Wallace's divergence idea in the interval.

claims.text: Brooks holds that Darwin may have received the letter as early as 14 May, and that he kept it for a month while revising his own manuscript.

disagreement.summary: Were the first five British editions reset, or printed from largely standing type? Peckham (1959) said the latter; Shillingsburg's bibliographical analysis says each was reset.

sides.position: Peckham: the text was not reset between editions; the printers corrected and reset only lines and paragraphs when necessary.

claims.text: Peckham stated that the printers treated Darwin's corrected copy of the first edition as another revise and reset only lines and paragraphs as needed.

citations.title: Introduction to the Online Variorum of Darwin's Origin of Species
citations.author: Barbara Bordalejo
citations.quote: The text, however, was not reset. The printers simply regarded Darwin's corrected copy of the first edition as still another revise.

sides.position: Shillingsburg: with minor exceptions each edition from 1860 to 1869 was completely reset, albeit line for line, so the 'standing type' account is impractical.

claims.text: Shillingsburg concludes that, apart from small exceptions in 1860, each new edition from 1860 to 1869 was completely reset.

citations.title: Introduction to the Online Variorum of Darwin's Origin of Species
citations.author: Barbara Bordalejo
